# 10 — bill of materials: one design, one parts list, ready to order and print

**Reference only. Do not edit this file.** Fill in `bom.csv`, `ai-log.md`,
`controller-comparison.csv` and `reflection.md` in this same folder.

You will work in **pairs** (ten pairs, ten drones). Together you finalize one
design and one bill of materials (BOM) that an instructor can order from and
that you can start printing. Every choice needs a reason you can justify.

## Your earlier choices are not locked

Your earlier work (`01` through `09`) is there to help you decide, not to bind
you. If you and your partner had different designs, choose one or merge them.
Change anything you like. **Every consequential change needs a row in
`DECISIONS.md`**: what changed, why, and the evidence.

## Pairs and repositories

- Students choose their own partner.
- The pair works together, and **both partners keep the same copy** of this
  folder in their own repositories. Put both names at the top of each file.

## Budget and scope

- **Budget: $500 per pair.** It covers everything you buy this semester,
  including filament (about two spools).
- The course provides chargers, test equipment and the Idea Shop printers.
  These are not part of your budget.
- **Buy only what is used this semester.** Motors spin in MMAE 477. The
  radio and receiver, and the companion computer and camera, are planned for
  later: do **not** put them in the "Buy now" section. List them in "Planned
  for later" with **mass and mounting information only**, so your frame leaves
  room for them and your mass budget includes them.
- The orders are placed after the BOMs are reviewed by the instructors.
  Every "Buy now" row needs a link and a price.

## Requirements

Your final propulsion choice should meet the five requirements from the
Electric Motors slides (on Canvas): hover thrust margin, hover duty cycle, ESC
rating, battery maximum current and hover time. They are listed on slide 32,
"Check every choice with the propulsion chain", the same as for Lab 08
(slide 18). Slides 21–26 work through them for an example quadcopter. If your
choice misses one, say so in `reflection.md` and say what you would change;
that is a valid result.

Check your choice yourselves with the propulsion chain from slides 27–29:
work out what your motor and propeller do at full throttle and at hover, then
compare against the requirements. Use any tool you like (a script, a
spreadsheet, a hand calculation), put it in this folder, and show where every
input comes from. **Include the mass of everything you will add later**
(receiver, camera, computer) in your total mass.

## Choosing the flight controller

Some potential controllers to explore are a **Pixhawk 4**, a Pixhawk-standard
controller such as the Pixhawk 6C, and a small 30.5 × 30.5 mm board or
"stack" (flight controller plus a 4-in-1 ESC) made for 5-inch quadcopters.
Consult AI to find and evaluate potential choices against the checklist below.

### What "firmware support" means

A flight controller is only a circuit board with a processor and sensors. What
makes it fly, and lets you spin motors from QGroundControl or Mission Planner,
is the software loaded onto it, called the **firmware**. The three main options
are:

- **PX4** and **ArduPilot**: autopilots with autonomy and support for adding a
  companion computer, which is what you will want in MMAE 478.
- **Betaflight**: made for hand-flown FPV racing.

The firmware has to be built for each specific board, because pin layouts,
sensors and memory differ. PX4 and ArduPilot each keep a public list of the
boards they build and maintain firmware for; those two pages are what the
checklist links to. If a board is on the list, you can install the firmware
from the ground software and it is kept up to date. If it is not, you may not
be able to install it at all, or only through an unofficial build that nobody
maintains. So your controller must run firmware that PX4 or ArduPilot
officially make for that exact board.

### Controller checklist

**Must have.** Your proposal must meet all of these, with a source for each:

1. **Firmware support.** The board is listed on the firmware project's own
   supported-hardware page:
   [PX4 flight controllers](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/flight_controller/) or
   [ArduPilot autopilot hardware](https://ardupilot.org/copter/docs/common-autopilots.html).
   A seller saying "PX4 compatible" is not enough.
2. **Fit and mass.** Mounting pattern and size fit your frame; mass is in your
   mass budget.
3. **Power.** Input voltage range covers your battery fully charged (4S is
   16.8 V).
4. **Motor outputs.** At least four. DShot (a digital ESC signal) is
   preferred, and bidirectional DShot, which reports motor rpm back to the
   controller, is a plus; PWM also works. If it is a stack, its ESC passes the
   requirement above: continuous rating ≥ 1.2 × your full-throttle motor
   current.
5. **Cost and delivery.** Fits the budget and arrives in time, from a seller
   with a track record.

**Recommended.** Say how your choice compares on each of these:

- **Room to grow.** Enough serial ports for a receiver, GPS, telemetry and a
  companion computer in MMAE 478, and an on-board 5 V supply that can power
  them.
- **Sensors.** An IMU and a barometer (standard on almost every board). A
  compass can be on the board or come later with a GPS module. Plan to
  soft-mount the board (rubber grommets) to keep motor vibration away from
  the IMU.
- **Support.** Plug-in connectors rather than solder pads, real documentation,
  an active user community.

Put two or three finalists in `controller-comparison.csv`, one row per
controller, scored against the checklist. Your proposal is the row you would
choose, with the reason in `DECISIONS.md`.

## Using AI to explore options

You are encouraged to use AI to find and compare options, especially for the
flight controller, where none of us knows the whole market. Use it to search
**wider**, then decide **yourselves**, with evidence.

You still need to:

- **log your decisions** in `DECISIONS.md`, with a primary source for each
  fact that drives them (the firmware project's supported-hardware page, the
  manufacturer's datasheet, a live listing). "The AI said so" is not evidence;
- **keep a short AI log** in `ai-log.md`: what the AI suggested, how you
  checked it, and whether you kept or rejected it. Catching an AI mistake is a
  good result.

## Steps

1. **Pair up and choose one design.** Note the design in `DECISIONS.md`.
2. **Propulsion first.** Choose motor, propeller, cell count, battery and ESC.
   Do the propulsion check. Iterate until the requirements are met, or you
   understand why they are not.
3. **Flight controller.** Explore with AI, fill `controller-comparison.csv`
   and `ai-log.md`, and choose your proposal. If you choose a stack, it
   replaces your separate ESC; check its rating again.
4. **The rest of the BOM.** Frame material and fasteners, wiring and
   connectors, filament. You may use AI to explore these too, in the same
   way.
5. **Planned for later.** Add mass and mounting pattern for each deferred part.
6. **Make the design ready to print** (see "Before you print"), and start
   your prints with the Idea Shop student workers. Printing can continue
   outside class.

## `bom.csv` columns

`section, part, qty, unit_price_usd, line_total_usd, mass_g_each, link, key_spec, reason`

- `section` is `buy_now` or `later`. For `later` rows leave the price and link
  empty and fill the mass and mounting information (put the mounting pattern
  in `key_spec`).
- `reason` ties the choice to a lecture idea or a check (for example: "KV
  chosen so hover duty cycle is 0.42, see our propulsion check").
- Add a final row `TOTAL` for the buy-now cost and the total mass.

## Before you print

Before printing, take every mounting dimension from a datasheet, and leave
adjustable mounts where a part (especially the flight controller) is not yet
chosen.

## Hand in

- `bom.csv`
- your propulsion check (script, spreadsheet or calculation), with sources
  for its inputs
- `controller-comparison.csv` and `ai-log.md`
- rows in `DECISIONS.md` for your major choices
- `reflection.md` (written together)

Both partners hand in the same files, in their own repositories.
